name: Guardrails for the Youngest Learners
title: Guardrails for the Youngest Learners
answer: For preschool through second grade, the book sets three firm guardrails: no facial recognition or camera based tracking of young children, no stored voice recordings unless a family agrees and there is a clear reason, and child mode turned on for every device young children use. These rules matter because the youngest learners cannot understand or consent to the sensitive data such tools collect, so the protection has to come from the school's policy rather than the child.

sections.body: This idea is a set of rules that carry extra weight in the early grades, where children cannot understand or agree to how their data is collected. The first rule bans facial recognition and camera based tracking, because tools that watch faces or movements to judge attention, emotion, or behavior gather sensitive information about children too young to consent. Instead, behavior patterns can be tracked through a teacher's own notes, with names removed before any AI tool is used. The second rule bans stored voice recordings, since speech tools need to hear a child to help but should not keep the audio after the session ends unless a family has agreed and there is a clear reason. The third rule requires child mode on every device, with the most protective settings on, web access limited, and AI features restricted to district approved tools.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In an early childhood program, these guardrails shape everyday choices about which tools are allowed and how they are set up. Teachers who want to note behavior patterns do it in their own written notes, stripping names before any AI tool touches the material, rather than relying on cameras to judge attention or emotion. When a speech tool is used to help a child, the session ends without the recording being kept, unless a family has agreed and a clear reason exists. Tablets and laptops for young children run in child mode, with the most protective settings on, web access limited, and AI features confined to tools the district has approved. The book presents these as rules for the preschool through second grade band, and says they are simple to state and belong in every early childhood program's written policy.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book offers one concrete sign that the concern about stored voice recordings is real: New Mexico's decision to let districts opt out of voice recordings in a statewide AI reading test, cited as GovTech, 2026. Beyond that example, the text does not present studies or figures for these guardrails. It also points districts toward a practical step rather than a research finding, namely asking every speech tool vendor how long recordings are kept and who can hear them. Figure 5.6 gathers the guardrails in one place. The text does not attach an evidence label to this idea, so it rests on practice and policy judgment rather than a body of research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are the guardrails themselves, and they are stated as firm rules rather than suggestions. Facial recognition and camera based tracking of young children are ruled out because the children cannot understand or agree to the data collection, and behavior tracking moves to a teacher's own notes with names removed before any AI tool is used. Stored voice recordings are ruled out after a session ends unless a family has agreed and there is a clear reason, and districts are told to ask vendors how long recordings are kept and who can hear them. Child mode stays on for every device, with web access limited and AI features restricted to district approved tools. The decisions that stay with people are the ones the text assigns to schools and families: whether a family agrees to a recording, whether a clear reason exists, and which tools the district approves.
